exercise1.prompt: original = [1, 2, 3], copy_list = original.copy(), append 4 to the copy, print both

hiddenCases.name: the two names point at two different lists
copy() makes the copy and append() adds to it

exercise1.hint: copy_list = original does not make a second list; it makes a second name for the first one, and appending through either name shows up in both. The proof is what original holds at the end.

exercise2.prompt: list1 = [1, 2, 3], list2 = [1, 2, 3]; print list1 == list2 and list1 is list2

cases.name: equal in value, but not the same object
cases.describe: True for ==, then False for is

hiddenCases.name: the two lists hold the same values
the two lists are separate objects

exercise2.hint: == asks whether two things hold the same values; `is` asks whether they are one thing with two names. Two lists typed out separately answer those two questions differently.

questions.prompt: After b = a, where a = [1, 2, 3], what does a hold once you run b.append(4)?
questions.explain: b = a copies the name, not the list, so both names refer to the same object and either one can change it.

questions.prompt: For list1 = [1, 2, 3] and list2 = [1, 2, 3], what are list1 == list2 and list1 is list2?
questions.explain: The values match, so == is True. They were built separately, so they are two objects and `is` is False.

questions.prompt: Which of these give you a list you can change without touching the original?
questions.explain: All three build a new list from the old one. Plain assignment is the only entry here that hands back the same object.

questions.prompt: You copy a list of lists with copy(), then change an inner list. What happens to the original?
choices: The change shows up there too, because the inner lists are shared
questions.explain: copy() is shallow: it makes a new outer list holding the same inner lists. Only a deep copy separates every level.
